title: Leaderless replication: quorums, hinted handoff and read repair
goal: By the end, you can explain how a store with no leader keeps three copies of each value, use R + W > N to predict whether a read must see the latest write, say how a copy that missed writes catches up, and name the cases where counting copies stops protecting you.
opening:
Picture a café owner checking her balance on her phone. A minute ago she moved 30.00 out of her account, and the app said OK. Her phone still shows 100.00.

Behind the app, each balance is kept on three computers, so one can break safely. None of the three is in charge. The app sends each change to all three and says OK as soon as one has it, because waiting for all three would slow every payment down. A minute ago, one of them was restarting. Just now, her phone asked that one.

It's tempting to think OK means every copy has the change. When one computer is in charge, you can ask that one. Here there's nobody to ask.

In Local-first software and sync engines, every phone was in charge of its own copy. In this lesson, we'll put nobody in charge. We'll count how many copies a write and a read must touch, break a cluster on purpose, and watch a stale copy catch up. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: The café's balance is kept on three computers, and one of them is switched off. The app writes a new balance, 70.00. It sends the change to every computer it can reach, and says OK as soon as one has stored it. Then it reads the balance by asking two computers and keeping the newer answer. What does the read return?
options: An error: with one computer off, a read can't ask two
70.00: only two computers are running, so the read asks both, and one of them had stored the change
Maybe 100.00: the OK only promised that one copy had changed
100.00, until the third computer is switched back on
warmup.why: Two computers are still running, so a read that needs two answers must ask both of them. The write said OK only after one of those two had stored 70.00, so the read always reaches a copy that has it, and the newer answer wins. "The OK only promised one copy" is the right worry in general: with all three running, a change might reach only one of them, and a read of two could pick the other two. Here the switched-off computer forces the read and the write to meet. The read would fail only with two computers off. Cassandra calls these two settings ONE and QUORUM, and the second section builds them up.

sections.h: Three copies and no leader: how long should a write wait?
sections.body:
Every lesson so far in this track had a leader: one computer that accepted each write and put the writes in order. In One leader, many followers, there was one for the whole database. In Many leaders and in Local-first software and sync engines, there was one per region or per device. This lesson removes the leader altogether.

Amazon did that in 2007, in a design called Dynamo, for the shopping cart on its website. Its target was strict: answer 999 of every 1,000 requests within 300 ms (thousandths of a second), even at the busiest hour. A leader gets in the way of a target like that twice. When it dies, writes stop until the others have chosen a new one, which is called an election. And when it's only slow, every write waits for it.

Dynamo's answer was to let any computer take any request. Each computer in the group is a node, and each copy of a value is a replica. The node that receives a request is the coordinator for that request. It sends the write to all N replicas of the value at once, where N is the number of copies, usually 3. Cassandra, a free database program that spreads its data over many computers, works the same way, and so do ScyllaDB and Riak, two programs built on the same design. The Cassandra docs say writes are "always sent to all replicas, regardless of consistency level", a setting the next section opens up.

No node is special, so there's no election. The coordinator can answer as soon as enough replicas have the write, so one slow machine holds nobody up. But nothing keeps the replicas in step either, so for a while they can disagree.

Think of three clerks in three towns, each keeping a copy of the same account book. You phone each new entry to all three. The question is how many must say "written" before you hang up. Each clerk is a replica, and you, making the calls, are the coordinator. Let's build the answer up with N = 3 and the café's balance. In the lab, the café's account is `A-1001`, and amounts are in cents, so 100.00 is `10000`.

Version 1 waits for all three. W is the number of replicas that must confirm a write, so this is W = 3. Every later read is then safe. But every write is as slow as the slowest of three machines, and with one replica down, nothing can be written at all.

Version 2 waits for one, W = 1. Writes are fast and almost always possible. But a read that asks a different replica from the one that answered can miss the write. That's the café owner's phone in the opening.

Version 3 waits for some, and that's where the read side comes in. R is the number of replicas a read asks. When their answers differ, the coordinator needs a way to pick one. So every value carries a timestamp, the time of its write, and the newest wins. Cassandra calls this rule last write wins.

**A write lands on some of the N copies, a read looks at some of them, and the read is right when those two groups overlap.** The rest of the lesson is about when they do. First, let's start a real cluster and find the three copies of one balance.

try.title: Start three nodes and find the three copies
steps: From the `labs` folder, start a cluster of three Cassandra 5.0 nodes, each in its own Docker container (a small, separate Linux system on your laptop): `docker compose -f env/cassandra-cluster.yml up -d --wait`. It takes about 3 to 4 minutes and about 3 GB of Docker's memory.

Load the table: `docker compose -f env/cassandra-cluster.yml exec cass1 cqlsh -f /sfz/nosql-06-balances.cql`. `cqlsh` is Cassandra's shell, where you type commands in CQL, its query language. The file creates a keyspace (Cassandra's word for a group of tables) called `payments`, with three copies of every row, and writes three balances, waiting for all three nodes each time.

Check the cluster: `docker compose -f env/cassandra-cluster.yml exec cass1 nodetool status payments`. `nodetool` is Cassandra's admin tool, and `UN` at the start of a line means the node is up and normal.

Ask which nodes hold the copies of account A-1001: `docker compose -f env/cassandra-cluster.yml exec cass1 nodetool getendpoints payments balances A-1001`. Leave the cluster running for the next three Try its.

refs.title: Apache Cassandra: Dynamo architecture (replication, consistency levels)

aside.title: Isn't DynamoDB the same thing as Dynamo?
aside.body: No, despite the name. DynamoDB is a database that Amazon Web Services, Amazon's business that rents out computers over the internet, runs for its customers. Its 2022 paper describes a leader for each partition, each slice of a table. The leader takes every write and confirms it once most of the partition's replicas have written it to their logs. Only the leader serves strongly consistent reads, the ones promised to see every confirmed write. So DynamoDB belongs with One leader, many followers, with a vote among the copies inside. Why other data models exist: Bigtable, Dynamo and the families made the same point.

sections.h: Count the copies: why R + W > N makes a read meet the write
sections.body:
Take N = 3, W = 2 and R = 2. The write is on at least two of the three replicas, and the read asks two of the three. Two plus two is four, and there are only three replicas, so at least one replica is in both groups. That replica has the write. Its timestamp is the newest the read sees, so the coordinator returns it.

In general, when R + W is more than N, every read meets every acknowledged write, one the client heard OK for. The reason fits in one sentence: you can't fit R + W different replicas into N. A group of replicas big enough to overlap every other such group is called a quorum. Why other data models exist stated the rule; now you can see why it holds.

Here are the choices for N = 3:

| W | R | R + W > 3? | good for |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | no | speed; reads may be stale |
| 2 | 2 | yes | the common default; one replica can be down for both |
| 1 | 3 | yes | fast writes, slow reads that need every replica |
| 3 | 1 | yes | fast reads; any one dead replica blocks writes |

Dynamo's paper calls (N, R, W) = (3, 2, 2) the common choice among Amazon's services. It also describes services that are read far more often than written, which set R = 1 and W = N.

R and W also decide what still works while nodes are down. A write needs W replicas up, and a read needs R. With one of three down, R = 2 and W = 2 both still work. With two down, both fail, and the coordinator refuses before it even tries.

Cassandra lets each request choose, with a setting called the consistency level. `ONE` waits for one replica, and `TWO` for two. `QUORUM` waits for a majority: half of N rounded down, plus one, so 2 of 3. `ALL` waits for every replica. `LOCAL_QUORUM` is a majority inside the coordinator's own datacenter, one building full of computers, for clusters spread over several. `ANY`, for writes only, accepts even a saved note for a down replica, which the next section calls a hint.

The defaults are low. `cqlsh` starts at `ONE`, and the Java driver 4.19, the library Java programs use to talk to Cassandra, starts at `LOCAL_ONE`. So you're at R = 1 and W = 1 until you choose otherwise. That's where the café in the opening was. Writing and reading at `QUORUM` gives 2 + 2 > 3.

The stepper runs one write at W = 1 with a replica down, then reads at R = 1 and R = 2. Watch the fifth frame closely. The R = 2 read is right there only because the write happened to reach two replicas, which W = 1 never promised. The last frame shows the run where it didn't. Then the Try it does the same on the real cluster.

sections.h: How a stale copy catches up: hints, read repair and anti-entropy
sections.body:
A replica that missed writes has to catch up somehow, or it stays wrong forever. Back to the three clerks. A clerk who was out for lunch finds a note on the desk. A clerk caught with an old entry is told the new one by whoever noticed. And now and then, the clerks compare their books and fix whatever differs. Leaderless stores do all three, each for a different case: the note is hinted handoff, the telling is read repair, and comparing books is anti-entropy.

Hinted handoff covers a replica that's down for a short time. When a replica doesn't answer, the coordinator keeps the write for it as a hint, and sends it over when the replica comes back. In Dynamo the hint goes to a stand-in node, as the stepper in Why other data models exist showed. Cassandra keeps it on the coordinator itself, in files named after the down node's host ID. The settings file `cassandra.yaml` in Cassandra 5.0.9 has `max_hint_window: 3h`. A node that stays down longer than 3 hours stops getting hints, and stays out of date until one of the other two ways reaches it.

Delivery is slowed on purpose, by default to 1024 KiB (about a megabyte) per second for each delivery thread, one path of work inside the program, so after a long outage on a busy cluster, the hints can take hours to drain. The docs call hints best-effort: Cassandra tries, but unlike repair, hints don't promise that the copies end up equal. A coordinator that is lost for good takes its unsent hints with it.

Read repair happens during a read. When a read asks R replicas and their answers differ, the coordinator writes the newest version back to the stale ones it asked, as in the stepper's sixth frame. Cassandra does it cheaply. One replica returns the data, and the others return only a digest, a hash of their answer. (A hash is a short fingerprint worked out from the data: the same data always gives the same fingerprint, and different data almost never does.) If the digests match, the read is done. If they don't, the coordinator fetches the full data, picks the newest and sends a repair.

At `QUORUM`, Cassandra waits for that repair before it answers. Afterwards a majority holds the new value, so any later quorum read meets it. Read repair only fixes keys that somebody reads, on the replicas that the read asked.

Anti-entropy covers the rest: rows nobody reads, and nodes that were down past the hint window. (Entropy means disorder, so anti-entropy is the work against it.) Two replicas compare everything they hold for a range of keys. Sending every row across to compare would be far too much traffic, so each replica builds a Merkle tree, a tree of hashes. The leaves are hashes of single keys, and each parent is the hash of its children, so equal roots mean equal data. When the roots differ, the replicas compare the children, and walk down only the branches that differ, until they reach the keys that are out of step (Dynamo, section 4.7). The figure shows one such walk.

A tree covers one range of keys, so when a node joins or leaves and the ranges move, the trees must be built again, a cost the Dynamo paper names. In Cassandra, anti-entropy is `nodetool repair`, which the people who run a cluster schedule to run regularly. Wide-column stores with Cassandra showed why that schedule has a deadline. A delete leaves a tombstone, a marker that says the row is gone. A node that misses a tombstone for longer than `gc_grace_seconds` (10 days by default) can bring the deleted data back. The Try it watches hints come home, then switches them off to catch read repair at work.

sections.h: Five cases where R + W > N doesn't protect you
sections.body:
R + W > N makes the read group and the write group overlap. It doesn't make three copies behave like one machine, and five cases show the gap.

The first is the sloppy quorum. Dynamo keeps each value on N particular nodes, its home replicas. When one of them is down, Dynamo writes to the next healthy node along its ring instead, and that stand-in counts toward W. A quorum that counts stand-ins is called sloppy. A later read that asks the home replicas can miss the stand-in completely, R + W > N or not. Cassandra doesn't count hints toward any level above `ANY`. That's one reason a Cassandra write can be refused where a Dynamo write wasn't.

The second is that a failed write isn't undone. If the coordinator gets fewer than W confirmations in time, the client sees an error. But the replicas that stored the write keep it, and later reads may return it. The Try it below makes one: a write at `ALL` fails with `WriteTimeout`, and the next read returns the "failed" value. So treat a timeout as "unknown", and make each retry idempotent: safe to repeat, because it carries a key that marks it as the same request. Rate limiting and idempotency keys, in the Caching track, built those keys.

The third is concurrent writes. Two people write the same balance at nearly the same moment. Both writes succeed, and the replicas keep the one with the higher timestamp. The other is gone without an error. Since timestamps come from clocks, a clock that runs fast decides who wins. Here the clerks stop being a good picture: a real clerk would notice two entries made at the same moment, and ask. The store keeps the later clock reading and drops the other without a word. The next lesson is about this case.

The fourth is reads during a write. While a write is still reaching the replicas, one quorum read can meet it, and a quorum read a moment later can miss it. Cassandra prevents that at `QUORUM`, because its read repair waits, as the last section showed. Daniel Abadi's 2012 paper on the trade-offs in database design puts it plainly: "simply using a quorum protocol is not sufficient" for linearizability. That's the promise that the store behaves as if there were one copy, and every read sees the latest completed write. Linearizability: one copy, one timeline, in the Consistency and consensus track, defines it properly.

The fifth is a copy that goes back in time. A replica restored from an old backup, or rebuilt from a stale neighbour, answers reads with old values that carry valid timestamps. The number of replicas holding a recent write can quietly drop below W until repair runs.

How often does any of this bite? Dynamo's paper counted the versions of shopping carts that clients saw over 24 hours. 99.94% of requests saw exactly one version, 0.00057% saw two, 0.00047% three and 0.00009% four. Failures and many writers on one cart caused the rest. That's rare, and Dynamo's carts kept every version for the program to merge, instead of dropping one. How much a rule loses depends on how often writes collide; whether it can lose at all depends on the rule.

So what should the café's app use? For a balance that decides whether a payment goes through, read and write at `QUORUM` (`LOCAL_QUORUM` with several datacenters), and make writes idempotent. Where two writers race on one row, use a lightweight transaction, Cassandra's "write only if the value is still what I read". The replicas agree on it first, using a voting method called Paxos, which Transactions in NoSQL covers. For data where a stale read costs nothing, such as a shop's daily totals that a program rebuilds every few minutes, `ONE` is fine, and it keeps working with two of the three replicas down.

Two questions remain open: how a node learns that another is down, and how a Cassandra cluster is wired together at all. The Partitioning track answers both, in Inside a Cassandra cluster: the token ring, gossip and failure detection. First, the Try it makes the second case happen: a write that fails, and lands anyway.

compare.title: Choosing R and W: Cassandra per request, DynamoDB per partition

a.label: Cassandra (leaderless)
a.title: cqlsh

b.label: DynamoDB (a leader per partition)
b.title: AWS SDK for Java 2.x

compare.note: Cassandra shows you the quorum arithmetic, and each statement chooses its own R or W. That's flexible, and it's also easy to get wrong one statement at a time. DynamoDB fixes the write side for you. Each slice of a table has a leader, which puts the writes in order and waits for most of the replicas, so you only choose how to read. An eventually consistent read, DynamoDB's name for a read from any replica, costs half as much and may miss a recent write. A strongly consistent read goes to the leader, which has every acknowledged write. Neither design lets two writers who race both win: Cassandra keeps the later timestamp, and DynamoDB applies the writes in the leader's order.

worked.title: Choose N, R and W for two payment tables

steps.say: Write down what each table must survive, and what a stale read costs. `balances` decides whether a payment goes through. `merchant_daily` holds each shop's daily totals, and a program rebuilds it from the payments every few minutes.
steps.code:
table               a stale read means               must keep working with
balances            approving a payment twice        one replica down
merchant_daily      a dashboard a few seconds old    two replicas down

steps.say: Balances: N = 3, so one dead node leaves two copies. R + W > 3, so every read sees the last acknowledged write. W = 2 and R = 2 both still work with one replica down. With two down, the app should refuse payments rather than guess, which is called failing closed.
steps.code:
N = 3, W = 2 (QUORUM), R = 2 (QUORUM)
2 + 2 = 4 > 3        -> every read overlaps every acknowledged write
one replica down     -> 2 alive, W and R both met
two replicas down    -> Unavailable: the service should fail closed

steps.say: The daily totals: staying available matters more than being up to date, and the next rebuild fixes everything anyway.
steps.code:
N = 3, W = 1 (ONE), R = 1 (ONE)
1 + 1 = 2, not > 3   -> a read may miss a recent write; the next rebuild fixes it
two replicas down    -> still readable and writable

steps.say: Put the choice in one settings file, not in every statement. The Java driver 4.x reads its settings from `application.conf`. A profile is a named group of settings: a statement that names the `money` profile uses its level instead of the default.
Every statement on balances names the `money` profile, for writes and reads alike, so nobody has to remember the level. Here's a read, in Kotlin.
steps.code:
val read = SimpleStatement
    .newInstance("SELECT balance_minor FROM payments.balances WHERE account_id = ?", "A-1001")
    .setExecutionProfileName("money")   // LOCAL_QUORUM: R = 2 of 3
val balance = session.execute(read).one()?.getLong("balance_minor")

lab.title: Build a quorum simulator with failures and read repair
steps: Run the tests from the `labs` folder. No Docker needed: the lab is a small model of a leaderless store that runs in memory. All nine tests fail with `NotImplementedError`.

Read `QuorumStore.kt`. The replicas and the functions `fail`, `recover`, `valueAt`, `subsets` and the private `storeIfNewer` are written for you. Every `write` and `read` names its own W or R, the way a Cassandra statement names its consistency level.

Write `write`. Refuse with `Unavailable` when fewer than `w` replicas are up. Otherwise stamp the next clock tick, store the value on every up replica in `reaches` (the replicas whose message arrives), and count the confirmations. Three tests pass, including the one where a timed-out write stays on the replica it reached.
Write `read`: ask the first `r` up replicas in `order`, keep the newest timestamp, and repair the stale replicas you asked. Five more pass.

Write `staleReadPossible` by brute force: try every write group and every read group that `subsets` gives you. The test checks your answer against R + W > N for every N up to 5. The last test runs 2,000 random steps of failures and lost messages at W = 2, R = 2. Change its `w = 2` to `w = 1`, watch it fail at some step, and put it back.
hints: `replicas.count { it.up }` is how many replicas the coordinator believes are alive. Check it before you touch `clock`.
`order.map(::replica).filter { it.up }.take(r)` is the group of replicas a read asks.
`maxByOrNull { it.timestamp }` picks the newest version. A replica with no version for the key counts as older than any version.
Repair with the given `storeIfNewer`, so a repair can never overwrite something newer.
In `staleReadPossible`, two groups miss each other when `readSet.none { it in writeSet }`. One such pair is enough to return true.

drill.title: The N = 3 table from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, fill in a table for N = 3, with a row for each (W, R) of (1, 1), (2, 2), (1, 3) and (3, 1). For each row, write whether every read sees the last acknowledged write, how many replicas can be down while writes still work, and how many while reads still work. Then write the one-line reason R + W > N works.

answer.src:
W  R   read sees last acked write?   down, writes work   down, reads work
1  1   no  (1 + 1 = 2)               2                   2
2  2   yes (2 + 2 = 4)               1                   1
1  3   yes (1 + 3 = 4)               2                   0
3  1   yes (3 + 1 = 4)               0                   2

Why: a write set of W replicas and a read set of R replicas can't both fit
into N replicas without sharing one when R + W > N, and the shared replica
has the write, with the newest timestamp the read sees.

recap: A leaderless store has no leader. The coordinator, whichever node got the request, sends every write to all N replicas and waits for W confirmations; a read asks R replicas and keeps the newest timestamp. No leader means no election, and no waiting on one slow machine.

R + W > N makes every read meet every acknowledged write, because R + W replicas can't fit into N without sharing one. For N = 3 a quorum is 2, and quorum writes and quorum reads both survive one replica down.
Cassandra lets each statement choose its W or R with a consistency level. `cqlsh` starts at `ONE` and the Java driver 4.19 at `LOCAL_ONE`, so you start at R = W = 1 unless you choose otherwise.

A stale copy catches up three ways: hinted handoff for short outages (3 hours by default in Cassandra), read repair for keys that get read, and anti-entropy, which compares Merkle trees of hashes, for everything else.

The limit: counting copies isn't a transaction. A timed-out write may have landed, one of two concurrent writes loses to the later timestamp, reads during a write can disagree, and a restored replica can go back in time. Dynamo saw a second version on only 0.06% of cart requests, but the rule decides what happens then.
closing:
We started with a café owner whose phone showed 100.00 after the app had said OK to 70.00. Her write reached one copy and her read asked another, and with R + W no more than N, nothing made them meet. Counting copies fixes that, apart from the five cases it doesn't.

Next time you start the lab cluster, type `CONSISTENCY` in `cqlsh` with nothing after it, and it prints the level you're at. Ask the same of any program that uses Cassandra: which level does it write at, and which does it read at?

Next, we'll take the third case apart. When do two writes really happen at the same time, and how can a store keep both?

quiz.q: A value has three replicas, N = 3. Writes wait for two confirmations, W = 2, and reads ask one replica, R = 1. Can a read miss a write that was acknowledged?
options: No: two replicas have the write, and two is a majority
No, as long as no replica is down
Yes: 2 + 1 = 3 is not more than 3, so the one replica a read asks may be the one without the write
Yes, but only while hinted handoff is switched off
quiz.why: The write group has two replicas and the read asks one. The third replica, which didn't take the write, is a perfectly good read group of one. A majority of writers isn't enough: the read group has to overlap the write group, which needs R + W > N. Hints don't change the arithmetic, and the miss can happen with every replica up, when one message is slow.

quiz.q: Three copies of every row, and two of the three replicas are down. Which still works?
options: Reads and writes at ONE
Reads at QUORUM, because one replica has the data
Writes at QUORUM, stored as hints
Nothing: the data can't be reached
quiz.why: ONE needs one live replica, and there is one. QUORUM needs 2 of 3 alive and gets 1, so Cassandra refuses both reads and writes with `Unavailable` before trying, as the second Try it showed. Hints don't count toward QUORUM; only `ANY` accepts a hint as a confirmation.

quiz.q: A write at ALL fails with `WriteTimeout: received only 2 responses`. What do you know about the cluster?
options: Nothing was written: Cassandra undid the write on the two replicas
The write is probably on two replicas, and later reads may return it; treat the outcome as unknown
The write is on exactly one replica, the coordinator
Read repair will remove the write, because it failed
quiz.why: A timeout means the coordinator stopped waiting, not that anything was undone. The two replicas that answered stored the value, and the last Try it read it back at ONE. Read repair spreads the newest timestamp, so it would spread this value, not remove it. Make the retry idempotent, so that running it again changes nothing.

quiz.q: Replica C is stale for two keys, A-1001 and A-2002. A read of A-1001 at QUORUM asks A and C, and repairs C. What happens to C's copy of A-2002?
options: It's repaired too: read repair fixes the whole replica
It's repaired at the next QUORUM read of any key
It's deleted, because C was found stale
Nothing: read repair fixes only the keys that were read, on the replicas that were asked
quiz.why: Read repair works on what the read touched: one key, and the replicas it asked. A-2002 stays stale until someone reads it from a group of at least two that includes C, a hint arrives, or anti-entropy (`nodetool repair`) compares Merkle trees for its range.

quiz.q: From Many leaders: geo-distribution and write conflicts. A DynamoDB global table keeps a copy in several regions; in MREC mode, every region takes writes. It and Cassandra at QUORUM each receive two concurrent writes to the same key, made at nearly the same moment with neither writer knowing of the other. What does each do with them?
options: Both keep the write with the later timestamp and silently drop the other
Both keep the two writes as siblings for the program to merge
MREC rejects one with ReplicatedWriteConflictException; Cassandra keeps both
QUORUM puts Cassandra's writes in order, so only MREC has a conflict
quiz.why: MREC settles each item by last writer wins on an internal timestamp, and Cassandra settles each value by its write timestamp: the same rule, one with many leaders and one with none. QUORUM makes reads meet acknowledged writes, but it doesn't put two writes in order. ReplicatedWriteConflictException belongs to MRSC, the strongly consistent mode, which checks with another region before it commits.

flashcards.front: What are N, R and W?
flashcards.back: N: how many replicas hold a value. W: how many must confirm a write. R: how many a read asks.

flashcards.front: Why does R + W > N make a read see the last acknowledged write?
flashcards.back: A write group of W and a read group of R can't fit in N replicas without sharing one, and the shared one has the write.

flashcards.front: What is Cassandra's QUORUM with three copies?
flashcards.back: 2 of 3. QUORUM writes and reads overlap (2 + 2 > 3), and both survive one replica down.

flashcards.front: What level do `cqlsh` and the Java driver 4.19 start at?
flashcards.back: `cqlsh`: ONE. The Java driver: LOCAL_ONE. You start at R = W = 1 unless you choose otherwise.

flashcards.front: `Unavailable` or `WriteTimeout`: which one may have changed the data?
flashcards.back: `WriteTimeout`. It was attempted and too few answers came in time, so the write may have landed. `Unavailable` means too few replicas were alive, and nothing was attempted.

flashcards.front: Hinted handoff, read repair, anti-entropy: what does each cover?
flashcards.back: Hints: a replica down for a short time (up to `max_hint_window`, 3 h). Read repair: keys that get read. Anti-entropy (`nodetool repair`, Merkle trees): everything else.

flashcards.front: Why doesn't QUORUM make Cassandra behave like a database on one machine?
flashcards.back: Timed-out writes aren't undone, one of two concurrent writes loses to the later timestamp, and reads during a write can disagree. Use idempotent writes and lightweight transactions.

terms.plain: Keeping copies where any node can take a write and send it to every copy, with no single copy putting the writes in order.
The node that received a request: it sends it on to the replicas, collects their answers and replies to the client.
Cassandra's setting, per statement, for how many replicas a write waits for or a read asks: ONE, QUORUM, ALL, LOCAL_QUORUM, ANY and others.
A group of replicas big enough that any two such groups share a member; with three replicas, any two.
Keeping a write for a replica that is down, and delivering it when the replica comes back.
During a read, writing the newest version back to the replicas that answered with an older one.
A background comparison of two replicas, range by range, that sends only the keys that differ.
A tree of hashes: each leaf is the hash of one key, each parent the hash of its children, so equal roots mean equal data.

explain_back.prompt: A friend says: "We write and read balances at QUORUM, so Cassandra is as safe for us as a database on one machine." Explain what that setting guarantees and what it doesn't.
explain_back.answer: With three replicas, QUORUM means two. A write is confirmed once two replicas have it, and a read asks two replicas and keeps the newest timestamp. Two plus two is more than three, so every read group shares a replica with every confirmed write, and the read sees that write. That's the guarantee, and it holds with one replica down. It doesn't behave like one machine, though. If a write times out, the client sees an error, but the replicas that stored it keep it, so the balance may have changed. If two people write the same balance at the same time, both succeed, and the replicas keep whichever has the later timestamp, so one change silently disappears. And in general, two quorum reads during a write can disagree, though Cassandra's read repair at QUORUM waits, which keeps a later read from going backwards. So we make writes idempotent, treat a timeout as unknown, and use a lightweight transaction where two writers can race on one row.

deeper.body:
How does a node know that another is down? (The Partitioning track covers this properly for Cassandra; here is the short version.) Dynamo's section 4.8 describes a gossip protocol: every second, each node contacts another chosen at random, and the two swap what they know about who is in the cluster. Failure detection is purely local in Dynamo: node A treats B as failed if B doesn't answer A's messages, whatever B looks like to others. Cassandra does the same with gossip. Every node runs a version of the Phi Accrual failure detector, which turns the gaps between heartbeats, the small "I'm alive" messages nodes send each other, into a level of suspicion instead of a yes-or-no timeout. That's why `docker compose pause` fooled the coordinator in the last Try it for a few seconds: a frozen program looks alive until enough heartbeats are missing.

Anti-entropy in practice, from the same cluster (output trimmed). With hints switched off, cass3 missed a write to A-2002 while it was stopped, and a full repair of the keyspace fixed it:

```text
$ nodetool repair --full payments
[2026-11-07 19:03:07,566] Starting repair command #1 (...), repairing keyspace payments with repair options (parallelism: parallel, primary range: false, incremental: false, ...)
[2026-11-07 19:03:07,998] Repair completed successfully
[2026-11-07 19:03:08,000] Repair command #1 finished in 0 seconds
```

After it, a read at `ONE` on cass3 returned the new balance. Real clusters run incremental repair, which only compares data written since the last repair, and schedule it with a tool, because a full repair of terabytes takes hours and every node takes part.

The Dynamo paper also has a small trick for reading your own writes. A write usually follows a read, so the coordinator for the write is chosen as the node that answered the earlier read fastest. That node then has the new version, and the client's next read is likely to reach it. It raises the chance of reading your own write without promising it.
